tip: Κλείνω (klíno) means close and also book: κλείσαμε καμπίνα (klísame kabína) = we booked a cabin.
Γυρίζω (yirízo) = turn, return and also tour: γυρίζουμε όλο το νησί (yirízume ólo to nisí) = we go all around the island.
Κάνει (káni) plus a time = it takes: κάνει δύο ώρες (káni dhío óres) = it takes two hours.
Οι αποσκευές (i aposkevés) = luggage – normally used in the plural in Greek.
Με συγχωρείτε (me sinkhoríte) = excuse me – a notch more formal than συγγνώμη (signómi).
Χωρίς (khorís) = without – it usually takes no article after it: χωρίς μετρό (khorís metró = without the metro).
Θέση (thési) = seat, job and also parking spot – context decides which one.
An adjective does the work of a whole English phrase: ήρθα όρθιος (írtha órthios), literally 'I came upright' = I rode standing the whole way.
Στις plus a time = at: στις δώδεκα και μισή (stis dhódheka ke misí) = at half past twelve.
Requests are often just the present tense with a question mark: μου δείχνεις; (mu dhíkhnis) = can you show me?
Yes/no questions keep statement word order – only the voice rises: αυτή είναι...; (aftí íne) = is this...?
Greek 'goes by' the stairs: πάμε από τις σκάλες (páme apó tis skáles) = we take the stairs.
Η έξοδος (i éksodhos) = exit is feminine, even though words ending in -ος (-os) are usually masculine.
Duration needs no 'for': κοιμήθηκα όλο το ταξίδι (kimíthika ólo to taksídhi = I slept the whole trip) – the time span just follows the verb bare.
Για να (ya na) = in order to: για να βρούμε (ya na vrúme) = so that we find.
Τα εισιτήριά μας (ta isitíriá mas = our tickets): a long word takes a second accent when μας (mas) is added.
Μπλε (ble) never changes form: την μπλε γραμμή (tin ble ghramí = the blue line) – borrowed colour words like this usually stay fixed.
Ο άντρας μου (o ándras mu) = my husband – literally 'my man'.
Age uses the of-form: δεκαπέντε χρονών (dhekapénde khronón = fifteen years old) is literally 'of fifteen years'.
Greek often doubles the article with names: η θεία μου η Σοφία (i thía mu i Sofía) = my aunt Sofia.
Greek marries 'with' someone, not to them: παντρεμένη με έναν γιατρό (pandreméni me énan yatró = married with a doctor).
Κάνω παιδί (káno pedhí) = have a baby: έκανε κοριτσάκι (ékane koritsáki) = she had a little girl.
Greek kids often get a grandparent's name: το ίδιο όνομα (to ídhio ónoma) = the same name.
Πώς λένε τον πατέρα σου; (pos léne ton patéra su) is literally 'how do they call your father?' = what's your father's name?
Greek names often have pet forms: the card's Μίμη (Mími) is the friendly version of Δημήτρη (Dhimítri).
Γιορτάζει (yiortázi) = he has his name day, from γιορτάζω (yiortázo) – often as big a deal as a birthday in Greece.
Της Παναγίας (tis Panayías) = of the Virgin: the of-form alone names the Aug 15 feast, one of the biggest name days of the summer.
On your name day YOU treat the others: φέρνει γλυκά (férni ghliká) = he brings sweets.
Θυμάμαι (thimáme = I remember) looks passive with its -μαι (-me) ending, but the meaning is plain active – a whole family of Greek verbs works this way.
Greek takes a phone to call someone: πήραμε τηλέφωνο (pírame tiléfono), literally 'we took a phone' = we phoned.
